newsitem.title: GERMANY: Battle-ready German steel workers return to work.
newsitem.headline: Battle-ready German steel workers return to work.

text.p: Thousands of steel workers at Thyssen Stahl AG who downed tools this week in protest against a hostile takeover bid by domestic rival Krupp returned to work on Wednesday on a limited basis.

After Krupp and Thyssen Stahl AG announced they would begin talks aimed at forming a joint steel company, possibly averting a hostile takeover, the works council said they would await the outcome of the talks.
Inspired by their fellow steel workers at Thyssen, thousands of workers from Krupp started staging stoppages, bringing to a standstill blast furnaces in Dortmund and steelworks in Bochum.

Krupp works council head Paul Ring said 6,000 to 7,000 workers had downed their tools because they were terrified of losing their jobs in Germany's smoke-stack industrial heartland in the Ruhr valley.

Thyssen Stahl works council head Dieter Kroll told a meeting of steel workers in Duisburg they should go back to work, but he warned managers they were ready at any time to down their tools again in protest.
Thyssen workers would return to work on Wednesday afternoon but it would take a couple of shifts to get back to full production probably on Thursday afternoon, Kroll said.
"We are ready to mobilise (stop work again) at any moment" Kroll told a gathering of workers after the meeting.
Thousands of steel workers at Thyssen and Krupp planned to join forces and hold a rally on Friday, Kroll said.
"We need the facts before us before we can decide on our position," Kroll said. "The problems won't just be wiped off the table. We are watching this process critically."
"I still can't believe that Krupp could try to take over Thyssen. That's like David taking Goliath," Kroll said.
Kroll said that although the proposed joint steel company was better than an all-out merger between the two firms, he thought over 5,000 jobs could still be threatened at Krupp.
"People are afraid and they are unsure," Kroll said.

Krupp and Thyssen have said they plan eight days of meetings to develop a common plan to create a jointly-owned steel company. Should those talks fail, the two companies would return to the starting blocks and Krupp would probably renew its offer to Thyssen shareholders.
Workers were suspicious about returning to work and said they first wanted to see soem concrete results.
"Why have we stood around here for two days if we're just going to go back to work? We should stay here until they have reached a final decision?" said steel worker Willi Wacker.

More than 6,000 angry steel workers from Thyssen downed tools and met at the vast Thyssen steelworks on the edge of the western city of Duisburg before marching to a hall in the centre to hear Thyssen Stahl chairman Ekkehard Schulz speak.

Schulz told the workers Thyssen planned to talk to Krupp about forming a joint steel group that would avoid a full-blown takeover. But workers said they feared thousands of jobs would still be at risk and vowed to continue their protest action.
Production remained at a standstill for the second day, but pungent smoke continued to belch from over 20 chimneys at the Thyssen plant as a skeleton staff tended blast furnaces.
